sources.text:
A US jury on Friday convicted a man of setting a New Year’s Eve fire that grew into one of several deadly blazes last year in Los Angeles, killing 12 people in the Pacific Palisades.
It was the second federal trial of Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, after the initial prosecution attempt left the jury deadlocked and ended in a mistrial.
The former Uber driver is scheduled for sentencing on March 17 next year. He faces up to 40 years in prison.
Photo: Reuters
Earlier this year, a separate jury leaned 10-2 toward acquitting Rinderknecht, but verdicts must be reached unanimously.
Jurors in the second trial were ordered not to take the previous proceedings or any mention of them into account in reaching their decision.
Friday’s verdict was on two charges: destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.
Rinderknecht had pleaded not guilty to both.
However, after approximately two days of deliberations, jurors found he used a lighter to ignite a brush fire in the vicinity of the wealthy, Malibu-adjacent Pacific Palisades neighborhood.
Firefighters had thought they extinguished the blaze, but later found that smoldering embers underground were carried by strong winds and erupted, tearing through the affluent area and ravaging thousands of homes.
It proved to be among the most destructive wildfires in California history.
Rinderknecht’s defense attorney, Steven Haney, had argued there was no direct evidence that his client started the fire, and said that errant New Year’s Eve fireworks could be to blame.
He said phone record evidence that Rinderknecht called 911 were efforts that he was trying to help alleviate the situation.
However, the prosecution said evidence including cellphone data put him at the scene of the crime.
They also pointed to a combination of video surveillance footage and analysis of fire spread dynamics to insist on his guilt.
The prosecution also said that Rinderknecht asked ChatGPT whether someone could be held liable for starting a fire with cigarettes.
One of the jurors, who identified himself as Cameron, told reporters outside the courthouse that while he had originally leaned not guilty, Rinderknecht’s interview with federal investigators was incriminating.
“It was a clear, calm night. You know, no one else was on that hill that day, or that day or night,” the juror said, but the defendant “happened to be smoking, and because he happened to be smoking, he had a lighter.”
“Everything kind of started to point towards one conclusion,” they said.
First Assistant US Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli lauded the verdict as “a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended.”
Fierce winds fueled the Los Angeles fires last year that resulted in 31 deaths.

sources.news_title: Federal Jury Convicts Former Los Angeles Resident of Starting Deadly Palisades Fire That Killed 12
sources.text:
LOS ANGELES — A federal jury convicted 30-year-old Jonathan Rinderknecht on Friday, Nov. 20, of deliberately starting a fire that authorities determined later developed into the catastrophic Palisades Fire, which killed 12 people and devastated thousands of homes in Los Angeles in January 2025.
The verdict followed a 14-day retrial in federal court after Rinderknecht’s first trial ended in June with a deadlocked jury. Jurors found the former Los Angeles resident guilty of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.
According to the U.S. Department of Justice’s announcement Friday, Rinderknecht faces a mandatory minimum prison sentence of five years and a maximum of 40 years. U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang scheduled sentencing for March 17, 2027.
The conviction concludes a second trial over the origins of one of California’s most destructive wildfires, which burned more than 23,000 acres, destroyed 6,837 structures and caused an estimated $25 billion in damage.
Attorney General Todd Blanche welcomed the verdict, citing the widespread destruction and loss of life.
“Twelve people lost their lives and thousands lost their homes because of Jonathan Rinderknecht’s malicious conduct,” Blanche said. “Thanks to the persistence and hard work of our prosecutors in the Central District of California, he will be held accountable.”
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli also credited federal investigators and prosecutors for pursuing the case following the initial mistrial.
“Jonathan Rinderknecht deliberately ignited a fire that killed 12 people and devastated an entire community,” Essayli said. “We were determined to hold him accountable, and today’s guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended.”
Federal prosecutors established that Rinderknecht started the Lachman Fire shortly after midnight on Jan. 1, 2025, in a secluded area of Pacific Palisades known as Hidden Buddha Hill, near the Skull Rock Trailhead.
Although firefighters initially suppressed the blaze, investigators determined that burning material remained underground in the roots of dense vegetation. Six days later, powerful Santa Ana winds caused the fire to resurface and spread rapidly through Pacific Palisades.
The resulting wildfire destroyed entire neighborhoods, forced widespread evacuations and became the most destructive fire in Los Angeles history.
Prosecutors presented digital evidence, cellular location records and testimony concerning Rinderknecht’s activities in the hours before the initial fire.
According to the Justice Department, Rinderknecht had been driving for Uber on New Year’s Eve 2024. Several passengers recalled that he appeared angry during their rides.
After dropping off his final passenger in Pacific Palisades, Rinderknecht drove to The Summit, a neighborhood where he had previously lived with a former romantic partner.
He then traveled toward the Skull Rock Trailhead, parked his vehicle and walked into the surrounding hills.
Prosecutors said he attempted to contact a former friend, recorded videos on his iPhone and listened to a rap song whose accompanying music video featured objects being set on fire.
Evidence presented during the trial indicated that Rinderknecht had been upset about personal relationships and difficulties finding companionship during the holiday.
Investigators determined that he was alone in a clearing when the Lachman Fire began shortly after midnight.
Environmental monitoring systems detected the fire at approximately 12:12 a.m. on Jan. 1.
During the next several minutes, Rinderknecht attempted to contact emergency dispatchers multiple times, but the calls initially failed because his phone was outside cellular coverage.
He eventually reached 911 after returning toward the bottom of the hiking trail, reporting the blaze after another resident had already notified authorities.
Prosecutors said Rinderknecht subsequently drove away, passing responding fire engines traveling in the opposite direction.
He then reversed course, followed the emergency vehicles back toward the fire and returned to the trail to observe firefighters responding to the incident.
Phone records showed that he recorded additional videos of the fire at approximately 1:02 a.m.
Federal investigators later examined discrepancies between Rinderknecht’s statements and the location information obtained from his cellphone.
During a Jan. 24, 2025, interview, he told investigators that he had been near the bottom of the hiking trail when he first noticed the fire.
However, cellphone geolocation data placed him approximately 30 feet from the flames while the blaze was rapidly developing, according to prosecutors.
That evidence became an important component of the government’s case connecting Rinderknecht to the initial ignition.
The defense challenged the prosecution’s conclusions, arguing that investigators had not directly observed Rinderknecht starting the fire and had relied heavily on circumstantial evidence.
Defense attorney Steve Haney emphasized that no eyewitness reported seeing Rinderknecht ignite the vegetation and that no surveillance footage captured the moment the fire began.
During the retrial, defense attorneys also raised the possibility that fireworks or another ignition source could have caused the initial blaze.
Federal prosecutors rejected those alternative explanations, maintaining that the physical evidence, witness testimony and digital records established Rinderknecht’s responsibility.
According to reporting by the Los Angeles Times, the jury deliberated for slightly more than two days before finding Rinderknecht guilty on both charges.
The conviction followed a substantially different outcome during his first trial earlier this year.
In June, a federal jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict after hearing evidence concerning the fire’s origin and Rinderknecht’s alleged involvement.
That jury was reportedly divided 10-2 in favor of acquittal, prompting the judge to declare a mistrial.
Prosecutors subsequently pursued a second trial, presenting their case with renewed emphasis on the sequence of events, digital evidence and expert testimony about the fire’s development.
The retrial began Nov. 4 and continued for approximately two weeks before the jury returned its verdict Friday.
The central issue was whether the relatively small fire that began on New Year’s Day remained active underground and subsequently developed into the devastating Jan. 7 wildfire.
Authorities determined that the initial Lachman Fire was suppressed at the surface but continued smoldering in underground root systems.
On Jan. 7, exceptionally strong winds spread the remaining fire through dry vegetation and into surrounding residential neighborhoods.
The Palisades Fire eventually consumed thousands of homes and businesses, displacing residents and destroying significant portions of the coastal Los Angeles community.
Investigators linked the two fires through their analysis of the ignition area, remaining underground combustion and the progression of the later wildfire.
The government’s case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, with substantial assistance from the Los Angeles Police Department and the U.S. Forest Service.
Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mark A. Williams, Matthew W. O’Brien and Danbee C. Kim prosecuted the case.
The verdict also brought renewed attention to the ongoing recovery challenges facing Pacific Palisades residents.
Many affected families have spent nearly two years dealing with damaged properties, insurance claims, rebuilding decisions and the financial consequences of losing homes or businesses.
Los Angeles City Councilmember Traci Park, whose district includes Pacific Palisades, described the conviction as an important development while acknowledging that a guilty verdict cannot restore what residents lost.
According to NBC Los Angeles, Park characterized the verdict as an important step but not the conclusion of the community’s recovery.
For survivors, the outcome addresses the criminal responsibility for the fire’s origin but does not resolve the broader consequences of the disaster.
The wildfire also generated extensive questions about emergency preparedness, evacuation procedures, firefighting resources and the ability of public agencies to respond to extreme wind-driven fire conditions.
Those issues remain separate from the federal criminal prosecution.
Rinderknecht, who has remained in federal custody since his arrest in October 2025, will now await sentencing.
The two convictions carry a combined maximum penalty of 40 years in federal prison, although the sentence will be determined by the judge after considering federal sentencing requirements and the circumstances of the case.
The Justice Department has established a process for Palisades Fire victims to receive information about the proceedings.
With the jury’s verdict, federal prosecutors have secured a conviction in a case involving the ignition of a wildfire that killed 12 people and caused one of the most extensive residential disasters in Los Angeles history.
Rinderknecht’s sentencing is scheduled for March 17, 2027, when the court will determine the punishment for the two federal offenses.

Jonathan Rinderknecht was found guilty of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce, according to NBC News.
He faces between five and 40 years in prison, with sentencing scheduled for March 17, prosecutors said.
The Palisades Fire, which erupted on Jan. 7, 2025, burned approximately 36.6 square miles, destroyed 6,837 homes, businesses and other structures, and caused an estimated $25 billion in damage.
Prosecutors said Rinderknecht was responsible for an earlier brush fire, known as the Lachman Fire, which subsequently reignited amid strong Santa Ana winds, developing into the devastating Palisades Fire.
During the trial, prosecutors presented surveillance footage, GPS location records and DNA evidence linking Rinderknecht to the initial fire.
His defense argued that no witnesses had seen him start the fire and that the initial fire scene had been compromised before investigators secured it.
Rinderknecht's first trial ended in a mistrial in June after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
"The question at the time was who was responsible. And now we have the answer to that question," First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli said following the verdict.
Los Angeles City Council member Traci Park said the conviction could not undo the devastation caused by the wildfire.
"There is no amount of courtroom justice that will ever undo the harm that was caused," she said.

He acknowledged witnessing the outbreak of the January 1 fire from the vantage point of a hill he had climbed to watch New Year’s fireworks. But Rinderknecht said he immediately called emergency 911 to report the blaze and remained at the scene until firefighters arrived and offered to help them.
Prosecutors have alleged that while placing his 911 call, Rinderknecht asked the AI app ChatGPT on his phone whether someone could be found at fault for lighting a fire “because of your cigarettes,” to which ChatGPT replied, “Yes.”

Jury finds man guilty in retrial over devastating 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles
After a mistrial earlier in the year, a new jury has found the man accused of starting the devastating 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles guilty.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST:
Palisades Fire was one of the most deadly and destructive in California history, tearing through Los Angeles County last year and killing 12 people and burning nearly 7,000 homes and businesses. Now a jury has convicted the man accused of starting the fire. This was a retrial because an earlier trial ended with a deadlocked jury. Steve Futterman has covered both and joins us now from LA. Steve, thanks so much for being with us.
STEVE FUTTERMAN, BYLINE: My pleasure, Scott.
SIMON: Tell us more about the jury's verdict yesterday.
FUTTERMAN: Well, it came on the third day of deliberations. The jury found Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty on two separate counts. Now, this trial involved the Palisades Fire, but it also involved a second fire, the Lachman Fire. Rinderknecht, who was an Uber driver at the time, was accused of starting the Lachman Fire just past midnight on January 1, last year. Now, the flames from that fire were put out, but it smoldered underground for a week, then reemerged a week later as that deadly Palisades Fire.
The prosecution's case centered on the fact that Rinderknecht was in the exact area where the fire was ignited at the time it was ignited. He was portrayed as an angry person, as a loner. The defense argued that the fire was started by New Year's fireworks, but there was a big problem - Rinderknecht himself told law enforcement before he was charged that he never saw or heard fireworks.
SIMON: Now, of course, a different jury earlier this year split 10-to-2 in favor of acquittal that led to a mistrial. How did jurors reach a different decision?
FUTTERMAN: Well, one of the charges was adjusted to focus only on the Lachman Fire. Some of the jurors in the first trial said they had problems with that argument that the Lachman Fire became the Palisades Fire. The prosecution also streamlined its case with less focus on personal attacks on Rinderknecht. Now, after the verdict yesterday, juror No. 3 spoke to reporters. His name is Cameron (ph). He declined to give his last name for privacy reasons.
CAMERON: The strongest evidence was the defendant's own testimony stating that he was up on a hill, didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks. It was a clear, calm night. You know, no one else was on the Hill that day. Logically, things start pointing towards him.
SIMON: Steve, what's the reaction been from those involved in the case?
FUTTERMAN: Well, the prosecutors were quite pleased with the decision. This is the first U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
BILL ESSAYLI: All of us remember the devastating images of people fleeing their homes, the fire destroying structures. And the question at the time was, who is responsible? And now we have the answer to that question.

JOEL RINDERKNECHT: They want him to be convicted, and it didn't matter. Ethics didn't matter. Misleading statement didn't matter. False statement didn't matter. The truth didn't matter.

RINDERKNECHT: Oh, I know he's innocent. It's not just a belief. I know he's innocent.

A federal jury in Los Angeles on Friday found 30-year-old Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty of intentionally sparking the initial blaze that erupted into the catastrophic 2025 Palisades Fire.
Following two days of deliberations, jurors convicted the former Pacific Palisades resident and Uber driver on both federal charges brought against him in the retrial: one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.
The verdict marks a major turn in the prosecution after Rinderknecht’s first trial ended in a mistrial in June 2026, when a previous jury deadlocked 10–2 in favor of acquittal.
Ahead of the November retrial, federal prosecutors streamlined their indictment by dropping a third charge of setting timber afire and narrowing the scope of the first count to focus specifically on the initial New Year’s Day brush fire, while the second count addressed the resulting Palisades Fire.
Rinderknecht showed little visible reaction as the verdict was read in court, briefly hugging his defense attorneys before being escorted out of the courtroom.
During the retrial, federal prosecutors argued that Rinderknecht, motivated by personal anger, loneliness and resentment toward wealth inequality, used a lighter to ignite dry vegetation along a remote mountainside trail near the Summit neighborhood of Pacific Palisades just after midnight on January 1, 2025.
Although firefighters quickly contained that initial blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, investigators determined that embers continued smoldering underground within the root system for six days.
Then, on January 7, 2025, powerful Santa Ana winds fanned the subterranean fire back to the surface, unleashing a massive firestorm that killed 12 people, destroyed 6,837 structures and caused an estimated $25 billion in damage — in the most destructive wildfire in Los Angeles history.
To establish Rinderknecht’s presence and state of mind, prosecutors presented an extensive trove of digital evidence, including phone geolocation data, Uber trip logs, 911 call recordings and thousands of interactions with ChatGPT.
Records showed Rinderknecht had dropped off an Uber passenger in the familiar neighborhood shortly before midnight and was at the hillside clearing as he placed more than a dozen 911 calls to report the flames.
Prosecutors also highlighted disturbing internet searches, angry text messages and a ChatGPT prompt in which Rinderknecht asked whether someone could be held liable for a fire accidentally started by a cigarette while he recorded firefighters battling the initial blaze. Following the disaster, Rinderknecht relocated to Melbourne, Florida, where federal agents arrested him in October 2025.
Defense attorney Steven Haney argued his client’s innocence throughout the proceedings, maintaining that investigators rushed to judgment without conclusive physical proof at an ignition site that had been walked over for days before being secured. The defense presented testimony disputing the government’s origin analysis and pointed to witness accounts of loud bangs and teenagers fleeing the area to suggest that New Year’s Eve fireworks were the true cause of the fire.
Following Friday’s verdict, Haney stated that while the defense team was disappointed by the outcome, they respected the jury’s lengthy deliberation and would evaluate options for an appeal.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli praised the verdict outside the courthouse, stating that the prosecution answered the long-standing question of who was responsible for the tragedy. Rinderknecht, who has remained in federal custody since his arrest last year, is scheduled to be sentenced by U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang on March 17, 2027.
Each of the two felony counts carries a mandatory minimum sentence of five years and a statutory maximum of 20 years, meaning Rinderknecht faces between five and 40 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. Juror says Rinderknecht's own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict
Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.

“Stating that he was up on the hill, didn’t smell a fire, didn’t see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night,” Cameron said.
Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been ‘mad at everything’
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”
Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

A jury in Los Angeles has convicted a former Uber driver of two federal arson charges for igniting the blaze that ultimately became the devastating Palisades fire.
Five months after jurors deadlocked in his first trial, a second US District Court jury found Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, guilty of destroying property by means of fire and arson affecting interstate commerce in the 2025 fire, one of the deadliest in California history.
Rinderknecht was found guilty of destroying property by fire and of arson affecting interstate commerce.
First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told reporters that Rinderknecht, who holds both American and French citizenship, could be imprisoned for as long as 40 years.
The Department of Justice said that, in the days leading up to the fire, Rinderknecht showed extreme anger, indignation, and frustration about being unable to find companionship on New Year’s Eve 2024 and about a former co-worker he briefly dated in March 2024.
Alone on New Year’s Eve, Rinderknecht drove several Uber passengers, nearly all of whom remembered him being angry that night.
He dropped off his final Uber passenger in the Pacific Palisades neighbourhood of Los Angeles and drove to The Summit, a neighbourhood where he had lived a few years earlier with a former lover.
Rinderknecht drove towards Skull Rock Trailhead, parked his car, attempted to contact a former friend, and walked up the trail before starting the fire.
Although crews quickly suppressed the initial fire, it smouldered underground for days before reigniting at the surface nearly a week later.
The flames were whipped by fierce winds into a conflagration that killed 12 people and laid waste to the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.
Some 6,800 homes and other structures went up in flames, with property losses estimated at $150billion.
The disaster coincided with another catastrophic wind-driven wildfire that erupted almost simultaneously in Eaton Canyon, about 30 miles (48 km) to the east, killing 19 people and ravaging the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena.
Fire investigators later concluded that sparks from an electrical transmission tower ignited the Eaton fire.
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS
Rinderknecht's defence attorney maintained his client was wrongly accused, suggesting the hilltop New Year's Day blaze was triggered by holiday fireworks and the massive Palisades inferno a week later was a separate fire set by someone else.
The opposing narratives of the disaster left the 12 jurors in the first trial deadlocked 10-2 in favour of acquittal and unable to reach a unanimous verdict on any of the three original charges.
Judge Anne Hwang declared a mistrial on June 26.
Prosecutors retried the defendant under a new grand jury indictment that dropped one charge altogether and modified the two remaining counts.
At both trials, prosecutors depicted Rinderknecht as a dejected loner harbouring deep resentment towards society, particularly the wealthy, who channelled his anger into a deliberate act of destruction.
Surveillance camera footage and mobile phone location data placed him as the sole person near the site when the initial fire broke out, prosecutors argued.
A green barbecue lighter found in the glove compartment of his rental car yielded DNA matching Rinderknecht's, the court heard.
Perhaps most strikingly, prosecutors alleged that while dialling 911 to report the blaze, he simultaneously asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"
Defence attorney Steve Haney maintained his client had been wrongly accused, pointing out that no witness saw Rinderknecht start the fire and no camera captured the moment of ignition.
Rinderknecht, a one-time Pacific Palisades resident himself who has remained in custody since he was arrested in Florida in October 2025, declined to testify in his own defence during either trial.
But he professed his innocence in a court declaration filed in March, denying he had willfully started any fire.
He acknowledged witnessing the January 1 fire from a hill he had climbed to watch New Year's fireworks.
However, Rinderknecht said he immediately called 911 to report the blaze, remained at the scene until firefighters arrived, and offered to help.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced on March 17, 2027.

The conviction ends a case that came close to collapsing. A first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June, and the judge declared a mistrial. The retrial began Nov. 4 and lasted about two weeks. Rinderknecht, a former Pacific Palisades resident who was working as an Uber driver, had pleaded not guilty.
Prosecutors said Rinderknecht deliberately lit a small brush fire, known as the Lachman Fire, in the early hours of Jan. 1, 2025, on a hillside above the neighborhood. Firefighters contained it at about eight acres, but prosecutors said it kept burning in underground root systems and surfaced again on Jan. 7, when hurricane-force Santa Ana winds pushed it into the Palisades Fire. The first count was narrowed to the New Year's Day fire. The second addresses the Palisades Fire itself. Prosecutors dropped a third charge, timber set afire, when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.
The Palisades Fire killed 12 people and burned through neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu. According to a Los Angeles Fire Department count, it destroyed 6,837 homes and burned 23,448 acres.
The prosecution rebuilt its case between trials. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said the indictment was narrowed to persuade jurors who might have been torn about holding Rinderknecht accountable. He said he believed the first jury acted improperly and considered matters that were not presented as evidence. Prosecutors also said the retrial avoided emphasizing Rinderknecht's resentment toward the wealthy and powerful, which they had earlier framed as societal revenge, and leaned instead on forensic and digital evidence.
That evidence included photographs showing his car parked at the base of the trail leading to the fire's origin, cellphone tower data placing him moving on the hill, and images from a fire-detection camera that prosecutors said showed the ignition window with no other cars or pedestrians approaching beforehand. Experts, prosecutors said, ruled out other ignition sources, including fireworks. Uber passengers and text messages to his girlfriend described him as erratic and angry before the fire. He called 911 more than a dozen times while walking down the hill. Prosecutors also presented his searches asking ChatGPT whether he could be at fault if a fire were started by his cigarettes, which they described as part of an alibi, along with ChatGPT-generated fire imagery they said showed his state of mind, a barbecue lighter found in his car, videos of firefighters, evidence that he returned to the scene, and testimony that he lied to investigators about where he had been.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams, who led the presentation of digital and forensic evidence, told jurors that Rinderknecht was "mad at everything, and frustrated." In closing arguments, Assistant U.S. Attorney Danbee Kim urged them to evaluate the evidence together: "Piece it together. Look at it as a whole." Essayli called the verdict a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case.
The defense argued that the case rested on circumstantial evidence. Attorney Steve Haney told jurors that no one saw the Lachman Fire start and no camera captured the ignition, and that there was no physical evidence of Rinderknecht using a lighter to ignite vegetation. He cited 67 lighter tests that he said did not show sustained fire spread. He said the hillside was publicly accessible until Jan. 7, that a neighbor reported seeing teenagers running from the trailhead, and that several witnesses reported a loud bang or explosion on New Year's Eve, which he said pointed to fireworks. Prosecutors said no fireworks appeared in thousands of images. Haney also said investigators never obtained Verizon records that could have shown whether anyone else was near the site, and that prosecutors had decided Rinderknecht was guilty and shaped the evidence to fit.
A retired U.S. Forest Service fire investigator testified for the defense that the origin area was different from the one prosecutors identified. Prosecutors accused him of perjury and asked the judge to strike his testimony. The judge rejected the request. Haney also told jurors to disregard evidence about Rinderknecht's character, calling it "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."
After the verdict, Haney said the defense was disappointed but respected the jury process, and that it would review appeal options "at the right time."
One juror, identified only as Cameron, told reporters that he was the only member of the jury who initially found Rinderknecht not guilty. One other juror was undecided, he said, and the rest believed Rinderknecht was guilty. Cameron said it "took a lot" to change his mind, and that he had initially been concerned about a "lack of information" on the defense's technical review. He said Rinderknecht's own testimony was the strongest evidence against him.
The criminal verdict settles who lit the first fire, in the jury's view. It does not settle whether the fire should have been out before the winds returned. Thousands of Palisades fire victims have sued the city of Los Angeles and the state of California. Alexander "Trey" Robertson, an attorney who represents about 3,300 of them, has said the plaintiffs do not allege that the city or state started the fire. Their claim is that embers from the Lachman Fire, which they say the state allowed to burn for six days on its land in Topanga State Park, amounted to a dangerous condition of public property. The state has said that putting out the fire was the fire department's job.
Questions about the mop-up of the Lachman Fire have also reached the city's own fire department. A 23-year Los Angeles firefighter, Scott Pike, said in sworn testimony in the victims' lawsuit that he warned a captain and other firefighters that more mop-up was needed on Jan. 2 and felt he was brushed off. Last year Mayor Karen Bass directed Fire Chief Jaime Moore to commission an independent investigation into the department's handling of the Lachman Fire. The city has also filed a cross-complaint seeking to make the state share any liability if the victims' suits succeed.
Rinderknecht remains free to appeal, and his lawyers have not said whether they will. The next court date in the criminal case is his sentencing on March 17, 2027. The civil suits against the city and the state continue on their own track, and their outcome does not depend on the verdict reached Friday.

The California man who sparked one of the deadliest and most destructive fires in the state’s history was found guilty by a federal jury Friday, months after his first trial ended in a mistrial with a deadlocked jury.
Jonathan Rinderknecht, also known as Jonathan Rinder or Jon Rinder, was found guilty of one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce after the 14-day trial, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ). Rinderknecht was arrested on October 7 after authorities tracked the deadly Palisades Fire to a smaller vegetation fire that had started early New Year’s Day last year.
Read More on News
According to the indictment filed in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, 30-year-old Rinderknecht started a fire near the Pacific Palisades neighborhood in Los Angeles, known as the Lachman Fire.
Officials say Rinderknecht had been working as an Uber driver the night before and after dropping off a customer drove toward Skull Rock Trailhead and walked up a trail. After the conviction, authorities said he had been exhibiting “extreme anger, indignation, and frustration” about not being able to find companionship for the holiday and about a coworker he had briefly dated.
Officials said that shortly after midnight, environment sensing platforms showed the Lachman Fire started and over the next five minutes, Rinderknecht attempted to call 911 but his calls would not go through because he did not have service.
He then got to the bottom of the trail and was able to connect with 911. Officials said he then left the scene, but turned around, following the fire engines and watching the scene unfold, taking videos with his phone.
The U.S. Attorney's Office says Rinderknecht lied about his whereabouts in an interview with law enforcement on January 24 of that year, but geolocation on his phone showed he was just feet away from the fire as it grew.
How the Lachman Fire Sparked the Palisades Fire
Fire crews believed that they had fully extinguished the small Lachman Fire; however, investigations later showed that the fire had been smoldering underground for nearly a week and sparked back up above ground on January 7. Strong Santa Ana winds and a nearly eight-month dry spell caused it to then explode into the Palisades Fire, which was active for 24 days.
Over the course of several weeks, the fire burned 23,448 acres, killed 12 people and destroyed 975 structures, according to Cal Fire.
Thousands of residents were displaced and the state is still trying to get enough funding to help Los Angeles rebuild after the coinciding Eaton Fire also destroyed homes.
According to an affidavit filed by a special agent with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives who handled the investigation, it was believed Rinderknecht started the fire using an incendiary device. The report says that while Rinderknecht told investigators during the January 24 interview that he occasionally smokes cigarettes, it was ruled out as a cause because they said the weather conditions at the time wouldn’t have triggered a fire.
The agent also said that while calling 911, Rinderknecht had asked ChatGPT, “Are you at fault if a fire is lift [sic] because of your cigarettes,” to which the artificial chat bot responded “yes” and gave an explanation.
While speaking to media outside a California courtroom this week, Steven Haney, Rinderknecht’s attorney, said prosecutors had presented the cigarette theory during the retrial.
“It was not something that was offered as a theory at the first trial, and it was clearly inconsistent with what they had been saying all along, is that it was started by a lighter,” Haney said, and that the theory showed “uncertainty” in what was believed to have caused the fire.
Newsweek reached out to Haney’s office via email outside of business hours Friday for comment.
How Many Years Can Jonathan Rinderknecht Serve in Prison?
Rinderknecht faces from five to 40 years in federal prison. He is scheduled to be sentenced on March 17.
"Today’s verdict delivers a measure of justice for the victims of this horrific tragedy,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement on X Friday.
Newsweek also reached out to Essayli’s office for further comment via email Friday.

UPDATED, 5:50 PM: A Los Angeles jury has convicted the man charged with setting the smoldering fire that later flared up into Palisades Fire that devastated Pacific Palisades and Malibu in early 2025. Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was found guilty Friday of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.
Rinderknecht faces a maximum sentence of 40 years in state prison when he is sentenced on March 17. He has been in federal custody since October 2025. See the bottom of this post for the the Justice Department’s detailed account of Rinderknecht’s movements on the night the first fire started and its case against him.
Back in June, a separate jury deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquitting Rinderknecht on similar charges including a third for timber set afire. Prosecutors dropped that last charge, and the In the new indictment, the first charge referred only to Rinderknecht’s setting of the Lachman Fire on New Year’s Eve, rather than the Lachman and Palisades fires. The Lachman Fire smoldered for a week before Santa Ana winds re-ignited the flames.
Watch on Deadline
During the just-ended trial, Assistant U.S. Attorney Matt O’Brien argued that Rinderknecht was consumed by anger, loneliness and a thirst for revenge, prompting him to use a grill lighter to ignite hilltop vegetation around midnight on Dec. 31, 2024, at the remote, deserted area adjacent to the Pacific Palisades’ Summit neighborhood. But defense lawyer Steven Haney argued there was no direct evidence proving that his client set the earlier fire, saying the prosecution’s case lacked any witnesses to the alleged crime and consisted only of circumstantial allegations.
The Los Angeles Fire Department issued in a statement Friday after the verdict. “We respect the jury’s work and the long, difficult process that brought us to today’s verdict,” it reads in part. “Our first thought is with the families of those we lost and for everyone in our community whose lives were changed by this fire. No verdict, however important, could ever undo that loss.”
The Palisades Fire was the most destructive blaze in Los Angeles history, killing 12 people, burning 23,448 acres, costing billions in damage and insurance claims, and ruining much of the exclusive Pacific Palisades community, destroying about 6,500 structures across the Palisades and Malibu. Read more details below, and see the full news release from the U.S. Department of Justice at the bottom of this post.
PREVIOUSLY, June 25: The jury charged with determining if Jonathan Rinderknecht is guilty of starting the blaze in early 2025 that became the devastating Palisades Fire can’t come up with a verdict, yet.
“The jury in the Jonathan Rinderknecht trial sent a subsequent note saying they are deadlocked,” the Justice Department tells Deadline today. “The trial continues.”
How long the trial continues now or if a mistrial is declared becomes the vital questions. U.S. District Court Judge Anne Hwang has instructed the jury to return on Friday morning to take another kick at the can.
A note from the jurors read out in court earlier this afternoon in downtown L.A. by the judge set the stage. “We have people on both sides that are dead set, unwavering and unwilling to change their opinion,” the note, the second of the day, said. It went on to say: “We are at a standstill and unsure of how to proceed.”
Ex-Uber driver Rinderknecht has always insisted he is innocent of the charges and being put up as a fall guy for the failures of civic leaders and First Responders. If a mistrial is declared in this instance, the feds could attempt another trial with a new jury and hope for a better outcome.
After just over a day of deliberations on the arson charges after a 10-day trial, the jurors indicated they had a verdict just over 90 minutes ago. The currently incarcerated Rinderknecht, his defense team, prosecutors and various local, state and federal officials were brought into court after the judge was informed there was a “unanimous verdict.”
What they finally did hear left Judge Hwang in clear angst.
While there was some confusion initially over when their decision would be read out in court, and the clocked ticked away, it is now clear the case is in serious trouble — even as it continues.
Looking at up to 45 years behind bars if found guilty, Rinderknecht was, in Department of Justice documents filed last fall, “indicted on one count of Destruction of Property by Means of Fire (18 U.S.C. § 844(f)(1)); one count of Arson Affecting Property Used in Interstate Commerce (18 U.S.C. § 844(i)); and one count of Timber Set Afire (18 U.S.C. § 1855), in a case arising out of the Lachman/Palisades Fire in January 2025.”
Today’s verdict or lack there of, will continue the frustration many feel over the wildfires, the response and the consequences. While some reconstruction has taken place in the Palisades, as well as Malibu and out of the Eaton Fire that tore through Altadena, progress has been slow and stymied by all metrics.
A major factor in the ongoing L.A. mayoral race, and the spark for the unsuccessful insurgency campaign of ex-Palisades resident and Hills alum Spencer Pratt, the fires and the fallout hang heavy over the city and the community as another sign of a metropolis that has lost its way — even more so this past week with the just extinguished cold storage warehouse fire in Boyle Heights that prompted air quality and other health warnings.
The subject of an intense investigation by various branches of government both national and state, Rinderknecht was arrested in Florida on October 8 last year. The then 29-year-old is accused of intentionally starting a “hold over” fire the week before that eventually sparked into the Palisades Fire.
Placed at the scene by his own iPhone and failed 9-1-1 calls, Rinderknecht later that New Year’s Day morning drove away from the area as LAFD started arriving on the scene, making a gesture to assist the firefighters, the DOJ’s filing of last year asserted.
A week later the same fire, which even after LAFD has been on the scene, had likely smoldered underground, reemerged and became known as the Palisades Fire. Destroying most of the Hollywood heavy community, the Palisades Fire killed more than a dozen people and decimated over 5,400 homes.
Earlier this week, after closing arguments, defense lawyer Steve Haney entered a motion to have the case dismissed based on lack of compelling evidence by the feds. With the bevy of online postings and asking AI platforms if you could start a fire with a lit cigarette, as well as Rinderknecht’s involvement with the January 1, 2025 Lachman Fire that preceded the Palisades Fire, that dismissal effort was dismissed pretty quickly by Judge Hwang.
More such motions from the defense may be in the offering ASAP if this deadlocked situation continues into next week.
Here is the Justice Department’s post-verdict news release:
	
A former Los Angeles resident was found guilty by a jury today of starting what became the Palisades Fire of January 2025, the most destructive wildfire in the city’s history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, a.k.a. “Jonathan Rinder,” and “Jon Rinder,” was found guilty of one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.
“Twelve people lost their lives and thousands lost their homes because of Jonathan Rinderknecht’s malicious conduct,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the persistence and hard work of our prosecutors in the Central District of California, he will be held accountable.”
“Jonathan Rinderknecht deliberately ignited a fire that killed 12 people and devastated an entire community,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “We were determined to hold him accountable, and today’s guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended.”
According to evidence presented at a 14-day trial, on January 1, 2025, Rinderknecht ignited what came to be known as the Lachman and Palisades fires.
In the days leading up to the Lachman Fire, Rinderknecht exhibited extreme anger, indignation, and frustration about being unable to find companionship on New Year’s Eve 2024 and about a former co-worker whom he briefly dated in March 2024.
Alone on New Year’s Eve, Rinderknecht drove several Uber passengers, nearly all of whom remembered him being angry that night. He dropped off his final Uber passenger in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles and drove to The Summit, a neighborhood where he had lived a few years earlier with a former lover.
Rinderknecht drove towards Skull Rock Trailhead, parked his car, attempted to contact a former friend, and walked up the trail. He then used his iPhone to take videos at a nearby hilltop area and listened to a rap song – to which he had listened repeatedly in previous days – whose music video included things being lit on fire.
When Rinderknecht maliciously started the Lachman Fire just after midnight, he was alone in a small clearing on Hidden Buddha Hill in Pacific Palisades.
At approximately 12:12 a.m. on January 1, 2025, environmental sensing platforms indicated the Lachman Fire had begun. During the next five minutes, Rinderknecht called 911 several times, but didn’t get through because his iPhone was out of cellphone range. When he finally connected with 911, he was at the bottom of the hiking trail and reported the fire. By that point, a nearby resident already had reported the fire to authorities.
Rinderknecht then fled in his car, passing fire engines driving in the opposite direction. He then turned around and followed the fire engines to the scene, driving at a high rate of speed. Rinderknecht walked up the same trail from earlier that night to watch the fire and the firefighters. At approximately 1:02 a.m., he used his iPhone to take more videos of the scene.
During an interview with law enforcement on January 24, 2025, Rinderknecht lied about where he was when he first saw the Lachman Fire. He claimed he was near the bottom of a hiking trail when he first saw the fire and called 911, but geolocation data from his iPhone carrier showed that he was standing in a clearing 30 feet from the fire as it rapidly grew.
Although firefighters quickly suppressed the Lachman Fire, the fire continued to smolder and burn underground within the root structure of dense vegetation.
On January 7, 2025, heavy winds caused the underground fire to surface and spread above ground in what became known as the Palisades Fire, which caused widespread damage in Pacific Palisades, killing 12 people, and destroyed 6,837 structures, causing an estimated $25 billion in damage in the most destructive wildfire in the city’s history.
United States District Judge Anne Hwang scheduled a March 17, 2027 sentencing hearing, at which time Rinderknecht would face a mandatory minimum sentence of five years in federal prison and a statutory maximum sentence of 40 years in federal prison.
Rinderknecht has been in federal custody since October 2025.
The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives is investigating this matter with substantial assistance from the Los Angeles Police Department and the United States Forest Service.
Assistant United States Attorneys Mark A. Williams, Matthew W. O’Brien, and Danbee C. Kim of the Environmental Crimes and Consumer Protection Section are prosecuting this case.
If you are a victim of the Palisades Fire, updates about this criminal case can be found on this webpage.
Erik Pedersen and City News Service contributed to this report.

Firefighters had thought they extinguished the blaze, but later found that smoldering embers underground were carried by strong winds and erupted, tearing through the affluent area and ravaging thousands of homes.
It proved to be among the most destructive wildfires in California history.
Rinderknecht's defense attorney, Steven Haney, had argued there was no direct evidence that his client started the fire, and suggested errant New Year's Eve fireworks could be to blame.
He said phone record evidence that Rinderknecht called 911 were efforts that he was trying to help alleviate the situation.
But the prosecution said evidence including cell phone data put him at the scene of the crime.
They also pointed to a combination of video surveillance footage and analysis of fire spread dynamics to insist on his guilt.
The prosecution also said that Rinderknecht asked ChatGPT whether someone could be held liable for starting a fire with cigarettes.
One of the jurors, who identified himself as Cameron, told reporters outside the courthouse that while he had originally leaned not guilty, Rinderknecht's interview with federal investigators was incriminating.
"It was a clear, calm night. You know, no one else was on that hill that day, or that day or night," the juror said, but the defendant "happened to be smoking, and because he happened to be smoking, he had a lighter."
"Everything kind of started to point towards one conclusion."
Nothing can 'erase the pain'
Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California, lauded the verdict as "a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended."
Fierce winds fueled the 2025 Los Angeles fires that resulted in a total of 31 deaths.
Alongside the blaze that devastated the Pacific Palisades, a second fire scorched Altadena, in northeast Los Angeles, razing parts of the neighborhood.
That fire was tied to an idle transmission tower owned by local power company Southern California Edison, whose sparks ignited dry vegetation.
Two years later, the city is still working to rebuild after the disaster.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass -- who just lost her reelection bid and was widely criticized for her handling of the fires -- said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured."

The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a “testament of the hard work” his team put into the case. He said he was “intimately familiar” with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht’s attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
“After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration,” Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favour of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.
Juror says Rinderknecht’s own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict
Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
“It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise,” he said. “After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he’s guilty.”
Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defence expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a “lack of information” presented to the jury about the technical review.
In the end, it was Rinderknecht’s own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.
“Stating that he was up on the hill, didn’t smell a fire, didn’t see fireworks . . . no one else was on the hill that night,” Cameron said.

sources.text:
A former Uber driver was convicted of a pair of federal charges Friday for setting a New Year’s Eve 2025 fire that smoldered for seven days before Santa Ana winds re-ignited the flames that became the Palisades Fire that destroyed much of the Pacific Palisades community and killed 12 people.
Jurors deliberated for about two and a half days before convicting Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.
Sentencing was scheduled for March 17, when Rinderknecht faces up to 40 years in prison.
Earlier this year, a separate jury deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquitting Rinderknecht of charges of destruction of property by means of fire, arson affecting property used in interstate commerce, and timber set afire.
Following that mistrial, prosecutors secured a superseding indictment with only two charges. In the new indictment, the first charge referred only to Rinderknecht’s setting of the Lachman Fire on New Year’s Eve, rather than the Lachman and Palisades fires.
During the trial in downtown Los Angeles, Assistant U.S. Attorney Matt O’Brien argued that Rinderknecht was consumed by anger, loneliness and a thirst for revenge, prompting him to use a grill lighter to ignite hilltop vegetation around midnight on Dec. 31, 2024, at the remote, deserted area adjacent to the Pacific Palisades’ Summit neighborhood. That fire was dubbed the Lachman Fire, named for a street near the Skull Rock Trailhead.
Prosecutors said firefighters initially thought they had extinguished the Lachman Fire, but instead it smoldered underground for six days in the root system of brushes and trees before bursting into view as the deadly Palisades Fire on Jan. 7, 2025, bolstered by strong Santa Ana winds.
But defense attorney Steven Haney argued there was no direct evidence proving that his client set the New Year’s Eve fire, saying the prosecution’s case lacked any witnesses to the alleged crime and consisted only of circumstantial allegations.
“There’s no direct physical evidence supporting their arson claims,” Haney told jurors at the onset of the trial.
Haney suggested the first fire was likely caused by errant New Year’s Eve fireworks. The defense attorney said Rinderknecht was on the trail near the Hidden Buddha clearing where the Lachman Fire was thought to have started, but he did nothing more than call 911 to report it.
O’Brien conceded nobody saw Rinderknecht start the fire, but he said witnesses, video surveillance, cell phone data and analysis of fire dynamics and patterns at the scene show he intentionally set the Lachman Fire then lied about it to investigators during an eight-hour interview.
The Palisades Fire was the most destructive blaze in Los Angeles history, killing 12 people, burning 23,448 acres, costing billions in damage and insurance claims, and ruining much of the exclusive Pacific Palisades community, destroying about 6,500 structures across the Palisades and Malibu.
One of the jurors, who identified himself only as Cameron, told reporters outside the courthouse that he originally believed Rinderknecht was not guilty, but he said as the jury discussed the evidence of the course of their deliberations he now believes he is guilty.
“The strongest evidence was the defendant’s own testimony stating that he was up on the hill, didn’t smell a fire, didn’t see fireworks,” Cameron, 30, said. “It was a clear, calm night. You know, no one else was on that hill that day, or that day or night, and (he) happened to be smoking, and because he happened to be smoking, he had a lighter.
“Therefore, everything kind of started to point towards one conclusion, especially if there was no one else on that hill, no fireworks, no electronic or no lighting strikes, like nothing else underground that was found through the tests and investigations.”
He said he could not say whether Rinderknecht had the intention of burning down Pacific Palisades.
“What I will say is that his intent was to start a fire. What that fire did after … only he will know and only God will know. And so the result of his fire is what ultimately led to January 7,” he said.
Rinderknecht’s father, Joel, told NBC4 after the trial that he still believes his son is innocent, and he called the verdict a miscarriage of justice. He told the station is was an impossible task to fight against the “steamroller” of the federal government seeking a conviction.
Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, called the verdict a “tremendous testament of the hard work that went into this case.”
“All of us remember the devastating images early last year of people fleeing their homes, the fire destroying structures,” Essayli said. “Twelve people lost their lives, 6,800 homes burned, $25 billion in damages. And the question at the time was who is responsible. And now we have the answer to that question.
“… I really, really want to thank the attorneys, the trial lawyers in my office who tried this case not once but twice,” he said. “A lot of people wanted us to just give up after the first trial, but we were confident in the facts.”
Kenny Cooper, special agent in charge of the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives in Los Angeles, credited investigators who worked on the case to determine the origin of the blaze.
“Using our state-of-the-art, world-renowned fire research lab, we conducted over 500 scientific experiments on some of the causes, potential causes of this fire,” he said. “Our national response team was brought in with subject matter experts, with certified fire investigators, our chemists, our engineers, our canine accelerant teams that came in. Hundreds and thousands of acres these investigators combed through to find the smallest pieces of evidence. We had over 17,000 items of evidence that we processed, over 1.5 million digital forensic data points to go through.
“… I can’t be more proud of the men and women in all the specialties that we brought to this investigation,” he said.
Haney told the Los Angeles Times he plans to appeal the verdict.
“We are disappointed in the verdict, but respect the jury process,” he said. “After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration.”
Rinderknecht has remained in federal custody while on trial because three separate judges found that he is a danger to the community. The findings were based on evidence showing, among other things, that he hid a firearm in a child’s teddy bear and threatened to burn his sister’s house down in Florida.
“While today’s verdict is an important step, it’s not closure,” Los Angeles City Councilwoman Traci Park, whose district includes the Palisades, told reporters outside the courthouse. “It’s not full accountability. There is still a lot more for us to do.”
She noted that a lot of progress has been made in the Palisades to recover from the fire, but much remains. She said the end of the trial “takes sort of one distraction off of a very crowded playing field of moving pieces.”
“You know, over the last 18 months, we have done an historic effort just with the debris removal, moving more debris out of the Pacific Palisades burn area than out of Ground Zero at 9/11,” she said. “We have in the last 22 months returned many of our schools and our local beloved businesses, and we see more and more families returning home. If you’ve been to the Palisades lately, you see the construction and the incredible momentum, and I see that too.
“… And for so many other victims of this fire, of the intentional conduct and choices that were made by one person that has caused so much harm, this struggle is far from over,” she said.

sources.text:
The man accused of deliberately setting the blaze that grew into one of the deadliest, most destructive wildfires in Los Angeles history was convicted of federal arson charges in a retrial of the case.
Five months after jurors deadlocked in his first trial, a second US District Court jury found Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, guilty of destroying property by means of fire and arson affecting interstate commerce in the 2025 Palisades fire.
The verdict came on the third day of deliberations.
Rinderknecht will be sentenced on 17 March.
First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told reporters that the defendant could face up to 40 years in prison.
Prosecutors streamlined their case in the second trial, focusing more on evidence that Rinderknecht was "the only person who could have reasonably, possibly" started the fire and that ruled out other causes, Mr Essayli said.
They characterised Rinderknecht, a former Uber driver of US and French citizenship, at both trials as a dejected loner who bore deep resentment against society, particularly the wealthy, and channelled his rage into an act of arson.
He was accused of "maliciously" starting a brush fire on 1 January 2025, that was quickly suppressed but smouldered underground for days.
Reignited at the surface nearly a week later, the flames were whipped by fierce winds into a conflagration that killed 12 people and laid waste to the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.
Around 6,800 homes and other structures went up in flames, with property losses estimated at $150 billion (€136 million).
Rinderknecht's defence attorney maintained his client was wrongly accused, suggesting the hilltop New Year's Day blaze was triggered by holiday fireworks and the massive Palisades inferno a week later was a separate fire set by someone else.
The opposing narratives of the disaster left the 12 jurors in the first trial deadlocked 10-2 in favour of acquittal and unable to reach a unanimous verdict on any of the three original charges.
Judge Anne Hwang declared a mistrial on 26 June.
Prosecutors retried the defendant under a new grand jury indictment that dropped one charge altogether and modified the two remaining counts.
The Palisades disaster coincided with another catastrophic wind-driven wildfire that erupted almost simultaneously in Eaton Canyon, about 48km to the east, killing 19 people and ravaging the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena.
Fire investigators later concluded that sparks from an electrical transmission tower ignited the Eaton fire.
Rinderknecht was the only person criminally charged in connection with either of the two 7 January blazes, which together rank as the deadliest wildfire incidents ever in Los Angeles County, surpassing the 29 lives lost in the Griffith Park fire of 1933.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
In court documents and public statements about the case, Mr Haney also suggested that his client was being scapegoated for failures of the Los Angeles Fire Department.
Mr Essayli said the judge barred the defence from presenting evidence that would have put the fire department on trial, a ruling that kept the focus on the defendant.
Prosecutors said security camera footage and location data from Rinderknecht's phone showed he was the only person in the vicinity of the 1 January blaze when it began near a trail in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
Rinderknecht, a onetime Pacific Palisades resident himself who has remained in custody since he was arrested in Florida in October 2025, declined to testify in his own defence during either trial.
But he professed his innocence in a court declaration filed in March, denying he had wilfully started any fire.
He acknowledged witnessing the outbreak of the 1 January fire from the vantage point of a hill he had climbed to watch New Year's fireworks.
But Rinderknecht said he immediately called emergency 911 to report the blaze and remained at the scene until firefighters arrived and offered to help them.
Prosecutors have alleged that while placing his 911 call, Rinderknecht asked the AI app ChatGPT on his phone whether someone could be found at fault for lighting a fire "because of your cigarettes" to which ChatGPT replied, "Yes".

LOS ANGELES (AP) — The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
Rinderknecht, with little apparent reaction, gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. His father was present for the trial and as the verdict was read.
Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by “societal revenge” like they previously did.
Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.
After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked. Jurors were instructed not to consider the Los Angeles Fire Department’s role in putting out the fire.
Rinderknecht’s defense attorney Steve Haney cast doubt on the government’s case and said that their evidence proves nothing.
Haney said the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was accessible to the public until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
“Six days of anyone and everyone walking across the spot the government now calls a crime scene,” he said.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.
Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”
Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, an ex-Uber driver accused of purposely sparking the deadly Palisades fire, was found guilty on Friday, Nov. 20 after a roughly three-week retrial.
Rinderknecht was charged with two arson-related counts, destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.
He was found guilty of both charges.
The jury deliberated for roughly 16 hours across three days.
Authorities accused Rinderknecht of setting the Jan. 1, 2025 Lachman fire, which smoldered underground for days as a holdover fire, reigniting into the massive Palisades fire on Jan. 7, 2025.
The Palisades fire was the most destructive blaze in Los Angeles history. It scorched over 23,500 acres in the Pacific Palisades and Malibu, killed 12 people and burned for over three weeks.
Rinderknecht was initially tried for three arson-related charges in June. That trial ended in a mistrial, with jurors split 10 in favor of not guilty and two in favor of guilty.
Ahead of the second trial, prosecutors revised charges against Rinderknecht, dropping a count of timber set afire he faced during his initial trial.
Federal prosecutors argued that Rinderknecht was alone on Hidden Buddha Hill as New Year’s Eve gave way to New Year’s Day, angry about his soured relationships, and that he used a neon green, long-handled lighter to start a fire that smoldered underground for days before reigniting into the Palisades fire during intense winds.
Prosecutors said the cause of the fire was determined to be an open flame, with all other possibilities ruled out by investigators.
Defense attorney Steve Haney argued that there was a lack of evidence that Rinderknecht started the fire, that it was possible others were on the hillside where the fire began that night and that a firework could have started the blaze.
Haney urged jurors to focus on evidence of arson, which he said was lacking, rather than Rinderknecht’s personal life, opinions or what the passengers he drove as an Uber driver thought about him.
One juror, a 30-year-old college student who identified himself only as Cameron, said the jury went into the deliberations with ten jurors believing Rinderknecht was guilty, one undecided and Cameron himself believing Rinderknecht was not guilty.
Speaking outside the downtown Los Angeles federal courthouse after the trial, Cameron said that during deliberations, he wanted to be sure that the investigation into the fire was not mishandled before he ultimately agreed that Rinderknecht was guilty.
“Strongest evidence was his, the defendant’s own testimony, stating he was up on the hill, didn’t smell a fire, didn’t see fireworks, it was a clear, calm, night, no one else on the hill, that day, that night and (he) happened to be smoking,” Cameron said.
“Therefore, everything kind of started to point towards one conclusion, especially if there was no one else on that hill, no fireworks, no electronic or no lighting strikes, like nothing else underground that was found through the tests and investigations.”
Rinderknecht did not testify during the trial, but recordings from interviews he did with law enforcement were played and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives agents testified about serving search warrants at Rinderknecht’s home, devices and car and interviewing him in the weeks following the fires.
Agents testified that Rinderknecht told investigators he was alone on Hidden Buddha Hill on New Year’s Eve, and that surveillance footage on the hill and phone records also showed Rinderknecht was alone on the hill where the blaze began.
Cameron said he could not say whether Rinderknecht had the intention of burning down Pacific Palisades.
“What I will say is that his intent was to start a fire. What that fire did after … only he will know and only God will know. And so the result of his fire is what ultimately led to January 7,” he said.
The Los Angeles Fire Department’s response to the Lachman fire garnered criticism from the public as the connection between that fire and the Palisades fire became known. Part of the jury’s instructions mandated the panel not consider if the fire department adequately put out the Lachman or Palisades fires in their decision.
Rinderknecht was not charged with any of the deaths in the Palisades fire, which were not allowed to be mentioned during the trial.
He remained in federal custody while on trial because three judges determined that he was a danger to the community. Evidence showed he hid a firearm in a child’s teddy bear and had threatened to burn down his sister’s house in Florida.
Rinderknecht’s father was in court for the verdict, and was consoled by another son, who placed a hand on his back. The father, Joel Rinderknecht, later told TV reporters outside the courthouse that the government constructed “a false narrative” about his son. “I know he’s innocent,” Joel Rinderknecht said.
The defendant thanked and hugged his lawyers before being returned to custody.
U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang will sentence Rinderknecht on March 17, 2027 at 10 a.m. He will face a minimum sentence of 5 years to a maximum sentence of 40 years in federal prison, according to Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California.
Essayli said his office believes that the jury in the initial trial in June did not properly follow the law and considered things outside of evidence, which is one of the reasons he decided the case should be retried. He said he was “intimately familiar with the strength of the evidence” of the case, which also contributed to his quick decision to retry it.
He said he was “startled” by some comments from jurors after the first trial. One juror referenced alleged negligence on the part of the fire department as a major factor, Essayli said, which was not part of the evidence that jurors had been given to consider.
He also attributed the second trial’s outcome to a more focused approach by federal prosecutors. “We decided to streamline the case,” he said.
Victims of the fire, meanwhile, continue to struggle.
“I don’t feel a sense of justice,” said Blake Armstrong, who lost his mobile home when the Tahitian Terrace Mobile Home Park on PCH burned in the Palisades fire. He can’t move back into the park until infrastructure is complete, he said, which could be in 2029.
“The issue is bigger than one person,” he said.
Denise Doyen, lost the Palisades home she lived in with her husband for 23 years.
“Yeah, I think I feel a smidge better that he is held to account,” she said of the verdict.
“He was so clear in wanting to hurt people in the Palisades and take vengeance on rich people. Then he ended up doing that,” she said. “It was an act of hate. His comments (overheard by his Uber customers in the car at the time) were so adamant … He was speaking in threatening terms.”
Doyen, 71, is a writer and lost all her journals, notes and research. Her husband, a book collector, lost about 6,000 books.
“Those bookshelves of ash were so strange. You could see the pages in the ashes. All that we will never get back,” she said.
They started rebuilding only recently, she added. A foundation was poured last week.
Essayli said his office has no plans to file charges against the Los Angeles Fire Department. The department’s response to the Lachman fire, the holdover fire that became the Palisades fire, and the Palisades fire itself has been the subject of heavy public scrutiny.
“It (the verdict) means Mr. Rinderknecht started the fire. This does not exonerate the city or any other actors and how they responded to the fire,” Essayli said.
He said that would be determined in other venues, referencing separate civil trials that are underway in connection with the Palisades fire.
“Both things can be true,” he said. “You can have an arsonist and you can have a less than adequate response by the fire department.”

“No amount of courtroom justice will ever restore what was lost or repair the harm that was caused,” said City Councilmember Traci Park, whose district includes the Pacific Palisades.
“While our justice system delivered accountability for the person responsible for starting the Palisades Fire, full accountability is far from over,” said LA County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath. “We have a responsibility to ensure survivors have the support they need to rebuild, including critical recovery funding from the federal government.
