The jury deliberated for two days before finding Rinderknecht guilty on the two counts of arson he was charged with.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams said in his closing statement Wednesday that Rinderknecht was angry and mad at everything when he dropped off an Uber passenger just before midnight in the Pacific Palisades, not far from where he had lived in a rented house with a former partner years earlier.
Surveillance camera footage from nearby homes, data from his cellphone and Rinderknecht’s own statements to investigators leave no doubt that he parked his car near a trailhead and hiked up in the dark to the so-called Hidden Buddha clearing in the hills above the houses, the prosecutor said.
A little after midnight, surveillance cameras designed to pick up early signs of wildfires recorded the first signs of a brush fire near the clearing where Rinderknecht’s cellphone data shows he was standing.
“We’ll never know all the reasons why he started the fire,” Williams told the jury, “but you’ve seen some of them.”
Rinderknecht was charged with two counts of arson, one for the Jan. 1 Lachman Fire and one for the Jan. 7 Palisades Fire, which broke out when extreme Santa Ana winds hit Southern California and reignited the embers that had been smoldering among tree roots for six days.
“We’re happy the jury focused on the evidence and came back with the right result,” Williams said after the verdict was returned.
The Palisades Fire destroyed thousands of homes in the wealthy enclave above the Pacific Ocean, as well in adjacent Malibu, and killed 12 people before it was contained on Jan. 31, 2025.
Prosecutors claim Rinderknecht was extremely agitated on New Year’s Eve, citing angry texts he sent to a girlfriend who had told him the night before that she needed space from him, as well as testimony from Uber passengers who rode with him that night and had to endure his rants.
After dropping a passenger off in the Palisades near where he had lived in happier days, the government says he hiked up to the Hidden Buddha clearing and used a large grill lighter that was later found in the glove compartment of his car to set fire to the shrubs.

In the end, it was Rinderknecht’s own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.
“Stating that he was up on the hill, didn’t smell a fire, didn’t see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night,” Cameron said.
Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been ‘mad at everything’
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by “societal revenge” like they previously did.
Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.
After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.
Defense argues fire's origin is unproven
Haney cast doubt on the government’s case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.
Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”
Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

A former Pacific Palisades resident was found guilty Friday of federal arson charges after prosecutors made a second attempt to convict him in connection with the 2025 Palisades Fire.
A Los Angeles jury found Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty of two charges: destruction by fire and destruction of property. Prosecutors alleged that Rinderknecht started a small fire, known as the Lachman Fire, that ultimately led to the devastating Palisades Fire.

Jurors reached the verdict at about 2:45 p.m. after deliberating for nearly three days following closing arguments Tuesday. The verdict came nearly five months after the first trial ended with a hung jury.
As the verdict was read, Rinderknecht, who was seated next to his defense attorney, Steve Haney, showed no visible reaction, although some reporters inside the courtroom gasped.
After the trial, Rinderknecht's father, Joel, told NBC Los Angeles that he still believes his son is innocent and called the verdict a miscarriage of justice.
He told the station that it was an impossible task to fight against the "steamroller" of the federal government seeking a conviction.
Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, called the verdict a "tremendous testament" to the hard work that went into the case.
"All of us remember the devastating images early last year of people fleeing their homes, the fire destroying structures," Essayli said. "Twelve people lost their lives, 6,800 homes burned, $25 billion in damages. And the question at the time was who is responsible. And now we have the answer to that."
LA City Councilmember Traci Park, whose district includes the Pacific Palisades, said the verdict is "an important step," but not a closure.
"It's not full accountability. There is still a lot more for us to do," Park said.
Mayor Karen Bass, whose absence during the Palisades Fire became a point of criticism during her mayoral campaign, released a statement saying, "Los Angeles will always stand with Pacific Palisades."
"Nearly two years ago, the Palisades Fire devastated our city, taking innocent lives, destroying thousands of homes, and changing so many lives and Los Angeles forever," Bass said. "No verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured. So many are still struggling to rebuild. For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Sentencing is expected to take place March 17, 2027. Rinderknecht faces a statutory maximum sentence of up to 40 years in federal prison.
Prosecutors alleged that Rinderknecht deliberately started the Lachman Fire, a small brush fire that broke out in the early morning hours of Jan. 1, 2025. They said embers continued smoldering underground for six days before reigniting amid gusty Santa Ana winds and sparking the devastating Palisades Fire.
To retry Rinderknecht, federal prosecutors revised the indictment and charged him with two federal arson-related crimes: setting fire to government property and setting fire to property used in interstate commerce.
When the retrial began Nov. 4, prosecutors zeroed in on digital and forensic evidence, including cellphone location data that they said placed him near the site of the Lachman Fire. Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams said fire-alert cameras showed the Lachman Fire igniting, with no other cars or pedestrians approaching the area before flames appeared.
The U.S. Attorney's Office again used Rinderknecht's ChatGPT search records during the retrial, alleging that the now-31-year-old had searched for information about whether he could have accidentally started a fire with his cigarette.
Williams also argued that Rinderknecht's previous ChatGPT-generated fire imagery offered insight into his state of mind and interest in wildfires.
During closing arguments, federal prosecutors reminded jurors that Rinderknecht had allegedly lied about his whereabouts when questioned by investigators and had a barbecue lighter in his car that could have been used to start the fire.
"Piece it together. Look at it as a whole," Assistant U.S. Attorney Danbee Kim urged jurors, asking them to evaluate all the evidence together rather than separately. She argued that Rinderknecht's anger, fascination with fire, return to the scene, videos of firefighters and alleged lies to investigators reinforced the forensic and digital evidence.
The verdict marks a victory for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California, which failed to secure a conviction in June after jurors deadlocked, resulting in a mistrial. The jury in Rinderknecht's first trial deadlocked 10-2 in favor of an acquittal. Prosecutors had immediately announced he would be retried.
The defense argued that prosecutors had predetermined Rinderknecht was guilty and then tried to make the evidence fit their theory without proving his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
Defense attorney Steve Haney pointed out that the prosecution's case was based largely on circumstantial evidence, as no one saw the Lachman Fire start and no camera captured its ignition. He also argued there was no physical evidence showing Rinderknecht using a lighter to ignite vegetation.
The defense also challenged the allegation that the fire was started with a lighter, citing 67 lighter tests. Haney argued the tests failed to demonstrate sustained fire spread.
There was also testimony that fireworks, explosions and flashes were reported during New Year's Eve celebrations before the Lachman Fire broke out. Defense attorneys have claimed that the Lachman Fire could have been started by New Year's Eve fireworks.
Haney has said there was insufficient evidence to prove the Lachman Fire was intentionally set and far from conclusive proof that embers reignited in the intense winds a week later.
Haney also told jurors that investigators failed to obtain Verizon records that could have shown whether anyone else was near the Lachman Fire site besides Rinderknecht.

Palisades Fire Arson Suspect Convicted on Federal Charges, Faces Up to 40 Years in Prison
A federal jury in Los Angeles has delivered a guilty verdict in the high-profile retrial of Jonathan Rinderknecht, convicting the 30-year-old former rideshare driver on two felony arson charges stemming from the blaze that erupted into the catastrophic Palisades Fire of January 2025.
The Verdict and Charges
Following a 14-day federal retrial and jury deliberations in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles, Rinderknecht was convicted on both counts presented in a superseding indictment: destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce. According to the United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California, United States District Judge Anne Hwang has set sentencing for March 17, 2027. Under federal law, Rinderknecht faces a mandatory minimum sentence of five years and a statutory maximum sentence of up to 40 years in federal prison.
The outcome delivers a definitive legal resolution following a contentious first trial over the summer that concluded in a mistrial when jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal. Federal prosecutors subsequently refined their charges and launched a second prosecution in November.
Evidence and Background
According to federal prosecutors, Rinderknecht maliciously ignited the initial brush fire—referred to as the Lachman Fire—in the early hours of January 1, 2025, in a clearing near the Skull Rock Trailhead above Pacific Palisades after completing rideshare shifts on New Year’s Eve. On January 7, 2025, powerful Santa Ana winds whipped the subterranean embers to the surface, sparking the Palisades Fire.
The ensuing wildfire tore through Pacific Palisades, Topanga, and Malibu, resulting in 12 fatalities, destroying 6,837 structures, and causing an estimated $25 billion in total property damage, making it the most destructive wildfire in Los Angeles history.
Throughout the trial, Assistant U.S. Attorneys presented detailed digital forensics, including iPhone carrier geolocation records that placed Rinderknecht within roughly 30 feet of the ignition site just as the fire broke out. The prosecution also introduced evidence showing that Rinderknecht filmed emergency personnel responding to the scene, conducted AI queries regarding fire-starting scenarios, and gave conflicting statements to federal investigators during initial interviews. While defense attorney Steve Haney argued that the government relied primarily on circumstantial evidence and maintained that New Year’s Eve fireworks could not be ruled out, the jury ultimately affirmed the government’s case.

The conviction closes a consequential legal chapter in one of the most devastating environmental and infrastructure catastrophes in modern Southern California history. Beyond its legal ramifications, the verdict provides judicial closure to thousands of displaced residents and families across the greater Los Angeles metropolitan area whose lives, communities, and creative spaces were permanently reshaped by the 2025 disaster.

Defense attorney Steven Haney argued that investigators failed to gather sufficient physical evidence and said that the Lachman Fire scene was not preserved until more than 10 days later, leaving the area accessible to the public and potentially compromised.
First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli addressed the outcome outside the courtroom.
“We were determined to hold him accountable, and today’s guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended,” said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California.
Essayli said his office was confident in the facts and chose to retry the case because they knew a fresh jury would return a guilty verdict upon seeing the evidence again.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass also spoke about the conclusion of the federal proceedings.
“No verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured,” said Karen Bass, Los Angeles mayor.
Los Angeles City Councilmember Traci Park, whose district includes Pacific Palisades, said the verdict does not constitute full accountability.
Court Schedules March Sentencing
Rinderknecht is in federal custody. Jonathan Rinderknecht is scheduled to be sentenced on March 17, 2027.
Pacific Palisades is a neighborhood in the Westside region of the city of Los Angeles, California, situated about 20 miles west of downtown. Founded in 1921 by a Methodist organization, the area has a long history that includes archeological evidence of Native American Indians living in the surrounding mountains for over 10,000 years.
During the period of Mexican rule, the land belonged to Rancho Boca de Santa Monica, granted in 1839. In 1911, film director Thomas Ince constructed his historic film studio Inceville in the Santa Monica Mountains, creating the first major development in the area since the Mexican rancho era and establishing a prototype for future Hollywood film studios.
He faces a mandatory minimum sentence of five years and a statutory maximum sentence of up to 40 years in federal prison. Assistant United States Attorneys Mark A. Williams, Matthew W. O’Brien, and Danbee C. Kim of the Environmental Crimes and Consumer Protection Section prosecuted the case.

On Friday, November 20, 2026, a federal jury convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, on two charges: destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce. The verdict came five months after his first trial ended in a mistrial when jurors couldn’t agree on whether he was responsible.
This time, prosecutors convinced the jury that Rinderknecht intentionally started a smaller brush fire that eventually turned into one of California’s most destructive wildfires.
The case dates back to January 1, 2025, when investigators say Rinderknecht started what became known as the Lachman Fire near the Pacific Palisades neighborhood.
Although firefighters initially brought the flames under control, authorities later determined the fire had never completely burned out. Instead, it continued smoldering underground inside vegetation and root systems for several days.
On January 7, 2025, powerful winds helped bring those hidden flames back to the surface, setting off the massive Palisades Fire.
The disaster burned more than 20,000 acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and caused billions of dollars in property damage. Entire residential blocks were reduced to ashes as residents scrambled to evacuate their homes.
Federal investigators eventually turned their attention to Rinderknecht, a former Pacific Palisades resident who was working as an Uber driver around the time of the initial fire.
Made to order and shipped to your door.
According to the Department of Justice, passengers who rode with him on December 31, 2024, described him as visibly angry and agitated.
Prosecutors said he later drove toward the Skull Rock Trailhead, parked his vehicle, and walked into an area near where the first flames appeared.
Investigators used cellphone location records, surveillance footage, witness statements, and fire analysis to build their case. Phone data reportedly placed Rinderknecht close to the ignition site when the blaze began.
Authorities also discovered he repeatedly attempted to contact 911 after the fire started. Prosecutors argued that those calls were part of an effort to make himself appear innocent.
During the trial, prosecutors introduced a question he allegedly asked ChatGPT shortly after the flames appeared: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”
Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams also described Rinderknecht’s emotional state before the blaze.
“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” Williams told jurors.
However, Rinderknecht’s defense team maintained that prosecutors had failed to establish exactly how the fire started.
His attorney, Steve Haney, questioned the reliability of the investigation, arguing that the original fire scene remained accessible to the public for nearly a week.
“Six days of anyone and everyone walking across the spot the government now calls a crime scene,” Haney argued.
The defense also suggested fireworks could have caused the initial blaze, pointing to witnesses who reported hearing a loud explosion near the area.
That argument eventually brought former NBA star Chris Bosh into the case.
Rinderknecht’s legal team attempted to introduce information from retired Cal Fire investigator Michael T. Cole, who suggested a firework may have been launched from a property owned by Bosh near the suspected ignition site.
Bosh and his wife, Adrienne, strongly rejected any suggestion that they were connected to the fire.
“To our knowledge, our Pacific Palisades property was unoccupied and was not being rented or used by guests during the time,” the couple explained in a statement.
“We have assisted the appropriate authorities by providing security footage in our possession and relevant information available to us.”
The couple also said their family was in Austin, Texas, when the initial fire began. Bosh has not been accused of wrongdoing or charged in connection with the disaster.
Despite the defense’s alternative explanations, the second jury sided with prosecutors.
The verdict marked a major turnaround from June 2026, when jurors in Rinderknecht’s first trial deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal, forcing a mistrial.
Rinderknecht is now scheduled to be sentenced on March 17, 2027. Each of his two federal convictions carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in prison.
For families who lost loved ones, homes, and entire communities, the guilty verdict marks a significant development in the lengthy legal battle surrounding the deadly wildfire.
